Capturing the Court

By: Kate Barry | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Judge Moseneke has recommended moving the seat of the Eastern Cape High Court to Bhisho. But who stands to benefit?

Unique Selling Point:
An interview with Jean du Plessis the owner of SKG and 50+ other companies. He owns the luxury Ebenhaeser Guest House spread over 3 properties overlooking the Nahoon River. SKG Africa is a massive property company based in East London. They own well over 600 properties throughout the country and have over 500 leases with government departments. For this, they earn well over R1.2 billion per annum.

In East London SKG built the massive Waverley Office Park which houses 22 public entities, including the Amathole District Municipality. They also house the Buffalo City Municipality in various city offices. So why did the ANC-led municipality agree to write off R50m owed to them by SKG Africa? And when the DA requested that the decision be rescinded, why did the ANC Mayor refuse to allow a vote?

Summary:
Research by the MHCAC released earlier this year found that if the move went ahead, one-third of Makhanda’s businesses would lose so many customers that they would have to shut down. Makhanda would become a “ghost town” where unemployment would skyrocket from 38.3% to above 50%, significantly higher than the national average of 33.6%. The research also found that more than 5000 people associated with different aspects of running and supplying the court would lose their jobs.

In Bhisho SKG Africa has been buying up office buildings and land, building an elaborate new office complex at Independence Avenue Office Park, and promising to refurbish the dilapidated Amatola Sun hotel and golf course for a cool R3 billion! But what it is it about Bhisho? Could he be positioning himself to accommodate the the dozens of new offices needed to accommodate the High Court move?
1. 25 offices for advocates
2. 40 offices for attorneys
3. 50 offices for the Master's Office
4. 20 offices for the NPA
5. 10 offices for the Legal Resources Centre
6. 10 offices for Legal Aid
7. 4 offices for the Sheriff

Further information:
In 2016 Jean du Plessis was a Director of a company called Mendo Properties. His co-director was the ANC's Chaplain General, Reverend Vukile Mehana.
Mendo Properties merged with Vukile Property Fund to acquire various properties in Bloemfontein (Fedsure Building), and Pretoria (Thibault Arcade, Koedoe Arcade, Polley's Arcade, Sancardia Building). A director of Vukile Property Fund is none other than Sedise Moseneke, the son of Judge Dikgang Moseneke.

Extra Budget Items:
Air travel to East London for 3: producer, camera man & presenter
Accommodation Makhanda & East London for 2 nights for 3 crew
Car Hire
Fuel
S&T for 2 nights for 3 crew

Script:


COURT IN THE MIDDLE – FINAL

V/O: Welcome to Bhisho, the provincial capital of the Eastern Cape.
And, if the Ministry of Justice has its way, the new seat of the Eastern Cape Division of the High Court.

Farenchia: I looked at pictures of Bhisho a couple of months ago, and I could not see myself there. Not at all.

Mabizela: If the relocation were to take place, infrastructure has to be built basically from scratch.

V/O: Makhanda, formerly known as Grahamstown, is one of the oldest cities in the province and historically the main seat of the Eastern Cape High Court. But now the City of Saints with its population of 140 000 is facing a significant and rapid decline because of a bureaucratic decision.

Vicky: It will completely decimate the economy of that town.

Alex: There's a lot of opposition to that move because it doesn't appear to be rational.

V/O: Our story looks at where the seat of the Court may be moving to, and the company that may be lucky enough to ultimately reap the benefits.

Vicky: There’s only about 11 000 permanent residents in Bhisho itself, most of which are government employees.

V/O: But an enterprise with a huge property portfolio is raking in hundreds of millions of rands in significant government contracts. And for some years they’ve been building in Bhisho. So, instead of improving access to justice, could the possible relocation inadvertently serve narrow business interests in Bhisho, and lead to the death of Makhanda?

Sfx: Look at the dates….1867

V/O; This is the Makhanda High Court library. An irreplaceable ree - source of case law spanning the last hundred-and-sixty years.

Sfx: It’s open to the public, to the Rhodes students, to the Rhodes Law Clinic. So…access to justice.

V/O: The court building still has solid yellowwood panelling and brass taps used for gas lamps in days gone by.
But to address the legacy of colonialism and apartheid, a committee chaired by retired Deputy Chief Justice Dikgang Moseneke recommended redrawing High Court jurisdictional boundaries in South Africa. When it came to the Eastern Cape, they dropped a bombshell.

Mabizela: The jurisdictional area of the Makhanda High Court would be drastically reduced to a mere 8%. That of course has a huge impact on the operations of this city.

V/O: Professor Sizwe Mabizela is Vice-Chancellor of Rhodes University. He’s also vice-chair of the Makhanda High Court Action Committee.

Mabizela: It will just be a matter of time before the court has to shut down completely because it will just become unviable.

V/O: The redrawn boundaries put 40% of the Eastern Cape’s population under Bisho’s jurisdiction in this central corridor. The reasons given are geographic proximity and shorter travelling distance to court.

Text: “Geographic nearness to institutions of justice …”
“…lessened travelling distance within the province.”

V/O: Makhanda will need far fewer judges, lawyers and advocates. To gauge the ripple effect on the town, the Action committee commissioned an economic impact study.

Mabizela: At the very least some 9405 jobs will be lost. That would be equivalent to about half a million jobs in Cape Town. Unemployment will soar, poverty will worsen. Food security for tens of thousands will be in jeopardy.

V/O: They invited Justice Minister Ronald Lamola to a public meeting in the City Hall last year, where they presented their findings. But in a written response to Carte Blanche, the Department claims the economic impact report cannot be relied on.

Text: The report’s methodology is premised on the impact of closing the High Court. As a result it is not a report that can be relied authoritatively (sic)

V/O: That’s a misinterpretation meant to discredit the report, says Mabizela.

Mabizela: With the greatest of respects, Minister has to accept that we commissioned a study because we didn’t want to suck things out of our thumbs.

V/O: With an 87% reduction in the caseload, one of the jobs at risk is that of Faren-chia Cummings, a legal secretary working for a local law firm.

Farenchia: Not only the legal secretaries, but co-workers from the Master of the High Court as well as the Directorate of Public Prosecutions – some of us will have to be retrenched, because everyone can’t move to Bhisho.


Masa: The lifeblood of Makhanda revolves around three things: excellent schools, Rhodes University and the Eastern Cape High Court. Now that the seat of the High Court might be moving to Bhisho, people are asking who stands to benefit?

V/O: Bhisho is an hour inland from East London. The High Court has three court rooms, but in 2022 the Department of Public Works put out a tender to renovate and expand the court, adding four more court rooms. The budget is over two hundred million, but the tender hasn’t been awarded yet.

Mabizela: The people who will benefit the most are people who will be involved in the development of the infrastructure. And I fear that there may well be all manner of shenanigans.

Alex: Because obviously in any procurement arrangement, the risk of corruption is significant.

V/O: Professor Alex van den Heever is from the Wits School of Governance.

Alex: That shift in itself doesn't appear to make sense from a public value perspective. And yet it's being done.

Masa: But to host the Seat of the Court is not just about a court building – it will require additional office space for more judges, advocates, attorneys, the master’s Office, the NPA, Legal Aid, the Sheriff. And Bhisho is not that big on office space.

V/O: Which isn’t to say they don’t have big dreams. The vacant land next to the Bhisho High Court has been earmarked for the R1.9 billion Bhisho Office Precinct.

Vicky: I’ve served on the Public Works portfolio committee for ten years now. In every State of the Province address we are promised that this term it is going to be finished.

V/O: Dr Vicky Knoetze is a member of the Eastern Cape Provincial Legislature.

Vicky: Nothing has happened on the issue of the Bhisho Office Precinct for the last ten years.

Masa: And how much money has been pumped into it?

Vicky: R65 million on consultants.

V/O: The Bhisho Office Precinct has taken more than a decade to get off the ground, or should we say to break ground. The Department of Public Works is awaiting Treasury approval for this public private partnership. The Head of Department is Thandolwethu Manda

HOD: We may have taken a decade, but we have never been this close as the Eastern Cape government.

Masa: Now, when we're talking about the millions that have already been spent on these professional quantity surveyors, engineers, architects and all of that, would you be willing to show us those drawings of what they have come up with?

HOD: Certainly, we would.

V/O: But now they say they’re not permitted to share the drawings with us. So, you’ll have to use your imagination.

HOD: That office is meant for seven head office departments. Once we complete ours, we will move our government departments to the State-owned.

V/O: But funnily enough, another Bhisho precinct was also conceptualised a decade ago, by a private developer called SKG Africa.
And today, rising out of the centre of Bhisho like a great colossus is what is now called the Independence Avenue Office Park. Eventually it will measure 100 000 square meters and is already occupied by four government departments.

Alex: It would require an upfront investment at risk. They must have had some certainty that they were going to have government clients. Bhisho is not a private sector city, it’s basically the government city. So, I would be very interested in what the overall strategy was there, and how they were certain they were going to have government clients?

V/O: SKG claim they weren’t certain. They simply determined the market requirements before starting construction in 2015.

Text: SKG commenced with determining the market requirements, whereafter construction started in 2015.

V/O: As it turns out SKG has a long-standing relationship with government. Based in East London, the founder is property tycoon Jean Du Plessis. He’s a reclusive figure who shies away from media attention.

Knoetze: He is director or is in some way connected to at least 63 companies in South Africa.

V/O: 2021 parliamentary records show some of the companies held over 500 government leases throughout the country. 200 were with the South African Police.
But SKG insists these records are wrong and they actually have well below 100 government leases. Naturally, we had to dig deeper…

Waverley Office Park in East London houses multiple public entities, while the Trust Centre building is home to the Buffalo City Municipality.
But in 2022, the Council gave SKG a R50million debt write-off from the 76 million owing for water, electricity, rates & taxes.

Masa: What incentive would that municipality have to gift SKG this?

Alex: None. No normal incentive.

Masa: And yet it was done anyway?

Alex: Municipalities have to protect their revenue and their budgets, and their expenditure and they have to prioritize greatest need. That seems very odd.

V/O: In a written response, the Municipality said Council took an Executive decision based on SKG’s Covid-19 relief motivation.

Text: Council took an executive decision to approve the writing-off of debt, based on the motivation provided by the customer.

V/O: We tried to interview SKG about their R50 million debt write-off and their investment in Bhisho.

Link: Initially they said it’s their company policy not to engage with media. Pretty odd for a company that does so much business with the government and gets so much of their income from public funds.

V/O: In a written response SKG states they had no prior knowledge about the possible move of the High Court seat to Bhisho. As for the debt write-off, they received no special treatment. They, like other companies, made an application in terms of the Covid-19 debt relief scheme available to all rate payers. They pointed out that another property company also received substantial debt relief.

Text: We are not involved in and do not know about the Court moving to Bhisho.

Text: Like other companies, we applied in terms of the debt incentive scheme. We were not party to the Council proceedings.

V/O: SKG claim they are merely a conduit for the collection of monies for services consumed by their tenants. Any debt relief ultimately benefited the tenants, and and not SKG.

Text: SKG is merely a conduit for the collection of monies for services consumed by its tenants.

Any debt relief under the debt incentive scheme is ultimately to the benefit of tenants who consumed services.

V/O: But on their application they included almost every property they own in Buffalo City - even the offices of the Municipality itself. Not to mention Mrs du Plessis’s guest house overlooking the Nahoon River.

Alex: Well, I think this would be a red flag. If I’m sitting in government and I see this at some public entity that this has happened, to me that red flag is there and suggests very strongly: investigate.

V/O: And that’s already underway, says the Municipality.

Text: The matter is currently the subject of an investigation.

V/O: Because back in Bhisho SKG’s government tenants, including the Office of the Premier, also benefited from the debt relief.

HOD: We are leasing for OTP, we’re leasing for Community Safety, we’re leasing for Social Development, and we have leased for recently, I think for Transport.

V/O: OTP stands for Office of the Premier, which already occupies an entire building next door to the new office park. The Premier is Oscar Mabuyane.

Masa: Doesn’t the Premier already have offices?

HOD: The Premier has got offices.

Masa: So why are we leasing more?

HOD: Because of the need.

Masa: For how much?

HOD: The easiest way of divulging that kind of information would be to follow the PAIA process.

Masa: But how come you can’t divulge how much? Because this is taxpayer’s money.

HOD: This is taxpayers’ money. But we can’t divulge a commercial information of the other party without the consent of the other party.

Alex: The public needs to know how its money is being spent. These are not necessarily business secrets in many respects. The government has to account for what it’s doing. It has to show that it’s doing things in a proper way.

V/O: The Minister of Public Works revealed that SKG received over R228 million in government rentals last year. Some of that was for the Office of the Premier. And it’s here that an investigation that began in Makhanda comes full circle: because if and when the government’s Office Precinct is finally built then SKG’s office park will have plenty of space to offer the privates sector should the seat of the High Court move to Bhisho.

V/O: With an 87% reduction in the caseload, one of the jobs at risk is that of Faren-chia Cummings, a legal secretary working for a local law firm. Farenchia: Not only the legal secretaries, but co-workers from the Master of the High Court as well as the Directorate of Public Prosecutions – some of us will have to be retrenched, because everyone can’t move to Bhisho. Masa: The lifeblood of Makhanda revolves around three things: excellent schools, Rhodes University and the Eastern Cape High Court. Now that the seat of the High Court might be moving to Bhisho, people are asking who stands to benefit? V/O: Bhisho is an hour inland from East London. The High Court has three court rooms, but in 2022 the Department of Public Works put out a tender to renovate and expand the court, adding four more court rooms. The budget is over two hundred million, but the tender hasn’t been awarded yet. Mabizela: The people who will benefit the most are people who will be involved in the development of the infrastructure. And I fear that there may well be all manner of shenanigans. Alex: Because obviously in any procurement arrangement, the risk of corruption is significant. V/O: Professor Alex van den Heever is from the Wits School of Governance. Alex: That shift in itself doesn't appear to make sense from a public value perspective. And yet it's being done. Masa: But to host the Seat of the Court is not just about a court building – it will require additional office space for more judges, advocates, attorneys, the master’s Office, the NPA, Legal Aid, the Sheriff. And Bhisho is not that big on office space. V/O: Which isn’t to say they don’t have big dreams. The vacant land next to the Bhisho High Court has been earmarked for the R1.9 billion Bhisho Office Precinct. Vicky: I’ve served on the Public Works portfolio committee for ten years now. In every State of the Province address we are promised that this term it is going to be finished. V/O: Dr Vicky Knoetze is a member of the Eastern Cape Provincial Legislature. Vicky: Nothing has happened on the issue of the Bhisho Office Precinct for the last ten years. Masa: And how much money has been pumped into it? Vicky: R65 million on consultants. V/O: The Bhisho Office Precinct has taken more than a decade to get off the ground, or should we say to break ground. The Department of Public Works is awaiting Treasury approval for this public private partnership. The Head of Department is Thandolwethu Manda HOD: We may have taken a decade, but we have never been this close as the Eastern Cape government. Masa: Now, when we're talking about the millions that have already been spent on these professional quantity surveyors, engineers, architects and all of that, would you be willing to show us those drawings of what they have come up with? HOD: Certainly, we would. V/O: But now they say they’re not permitted to share the drawings with us. So, you’ll have to use your imagination. HOD: That office is meant for seven head office departments. Once we complete ours, we will move our government departments to the State-owned. V/O: But funnily enough, another Bhisho precinct was also conceptualised a decade ago, by a private developer called SKG Africa. And today, rising out of the centre of Bhisho like a great colossus is what is now called the Independence Avenue Office Park. Eventually it will measure 100 000 square meters and is already occupied by four government departments. Alex: It would require an upfront investment at risk. They must have had some certainty that they were going to have government clients. Bhisho is not a private sector city, it’s basically the government city. So, I would be very interested in what the overall strategy was there, and how they were certain they were going to have government clients? V/O: SKG claim they weren’t certain. They simply determined the market requirements before starting construction in 2015. Text: SKG commenced with determining the market requirements, whereafter construction started in 2015. V/O: As it turns out SKG has a long-standing relationship with government. Based in East London, the founder is property tycoon Jean Du Plessis. He’s a reclusive figure who shies away from media attention. Knoetze: He is director or is in some way connected to at least 63 companies in South Africa. V/O: 2021 parliamentary records show some of the companies held over 500 government leases throughout the country. 200 were with the South African Police. But SKG insists these records are wrong and they actually have well below 100 government leases. Naturally, we had to dig deeper… Waverley Office Park in East London houses multiple public entities, while the Trust Centre building is home to the Buffalo City Municipality. But in 2022, the Council gave SKG a R50million debt write-off from the 76 million owing for water, electricity, rates & taxes. Masa: What incentive would that municipality have to gift SKG this? Alex: None. No normal incentive. Masa: And yet it was done anyway? Alex: Municipalities have to protect their revenue and their budgets, and their expenditure and they have to prioritize greatest need. That seems very odd. V/O: In a written response, the Municipality said Council took an Executive decision based on SKG’s Covid-19 relief motivation. Text: Council took an executive decision to approve the writing-off of debt, based on the motivation provided by the customer. V/O: We tried to interview SKG about their R50 million debt write-off and their investment in Bhisho. Link: Initially they said it’s their company policy not to engage with media. Pretty odd for a company that does so much business with the government and gets so much of their income from public funds. V/O: In a written response SKG states they had no prior knowledge about the possible move of the High Court seat to Bhisho. As for the debt write-off, they received no special treatment. They, like other companies, made an application in terms of the Covid-19 debt relief scheme available to all rate payers. They pointed out that another property company also received substantial debt relief. Text: We are not involved in and do not know about the Court moving to Bhisho. Text: Like other companies, we applied in terms of the debt incentive scheme. We were not party to the Council proceedings. V/O: SKG claim they are merely a conduit for the collection of monies for services consumed by their tenants. Any debt relief ultimately benefited the tenants, and and not SKG. Text: SKG is merely a conduit for the collection of monies for services consumed by its tenants. Any debt relief under the debt incentive scheme is ultimately to the benefit of tenants who consumed services. V/O: But on their application they included almost every property they own in Buffalo City - even the offices of the Municipality itself. Not to mention Mrs du Plessis’s guest house overlooking the Nahoon River. Alex: Well, I think this would be a red flag. If I’m sitting in government and I see this at some public entity that this has happened, to me that red flag is there and suggests very strongly: investigate. V/O: And that’s already underway, says the Municipality. Text: The matter is currently the subject of an investigation. V/O: Because back in Bhisho SKG’s government tenants, including the Office of the Premier, also benefited from the debt relief. HOD: We are leasing for OTP, we’re leasing for Community Safety, we’re leasing for Social Development, and we have leased for recently, I think for Transport. V/O: OTP stands for Office of the Premier, which already occupies an entire building next door to the new office park. The Premier is Oscar Mabuyane. Masa: Doesn’t the Premier already have offices? HOD: The Premier has got offices. Masa: So why are we leasing more? HOD: Because of the need. Masa: For how much? HOD: The easiest way of divulging that kind of information would be to follow the PAIA process. Masa: But how come you can’t divulge how much? Because this is taxpayer’s money. HOD: This is taxpayers’ money. But we can’t divulge a commercial information of the other party without the consent of the other party. Alex: The public needs to know how its money is being spent. These are not necessarily business secrets in many respects. The government has to account for what it’s doing. It has to show that it’s doing things in a proper way. V/O: The Minister of Public Works revealed that SKG received over R228 million in government rentals last year. Some of that was for the Office of the Premier. And it’s here that an investigation that began in Makhanda comes full circle: because if and when the government’s Office Precinct is finally built then SKG’s office park will have plenty of space to offer the privates sector should the seat of the High Court move to Bhisho.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Judge Moseneke has recommended moving the seat of the Eastern Cape High Court to Bhisho. But who stands to benefit?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: An interview with Jean du Plessis the owner of SKG and 50+ other companies. He owns the luxury Ebenhaeser Guest House spread over 3 properties overlooking the Nahoon River. SKG Africa is a massive property company based in East London. They own well over 600 properties throughout the country and have over 500 leases with government departments. For this, they earn well over R1.2 billion per annum. In East London SKG built the massive Waverley Office Park which houses 22 public entities, including the Amathole District Municipality. They also house the Buffalo City Municipality in various city offices. So why did the ANC-led municipality agree to write off R50m owed to them by SKG Africa? And when the DA requested that the decision be rescinded, why did the ANC Mayor refuse to allow a vote?
metadata.Summary: Research by the MHCAC released earlier this year found that if the move went ahead, one-third of Makhanda’s businesses would lose so many customers that they would have to shut down. Makhanda would become a “ghost town” where unemployment would skyrocket from 38.3% to above 50%, significantly higher than the national average of 33.6%. The research also found that more than 5000 people associated with different aspects of running and supplying the court would lose their jobs. In Bhisho SKG Africa has been buying up office buildings and land, building an elaborate new office complex at Independence Avenue Office Park, and promising to refurbish the dilapidated Amatola Sun hotel and golf course for a cool R3 billion! But what it is it about Bhisho? Could he be positioning himself to accommodate the the dozens of new offices needed to accommodate the High Court move? 1. 25 offices for advocates 2. 40 offices for attorneys 3. 50 offices for the Master's Office 4. 20 offices for the NPA 5. 10 offices for the Legal Resources Centre 6. 10 offices for Legal Aid 7. 4 offices for the Sheriff
metadata.Further information: In 2016 Jean du Plessis was a Director of a company called Mendo Properties. His co-director was the ANC's Chaplain General, Reverend Vukile Mehana. Mendo Properties merged with Vukile Property Fund to acquire various properties in Bloemfontein (Fedsure Building), and Pretoria (Thibault Arcade, Koedoe Arcade, Polley's Arcade, Sancardia Building). A director of Vukile Property Fund is none other than Sedise Moseneke, the son of Judge Dikgang Moseneke.
